sectionToMerge.h2: Frequently Asked Questions About Hepatic Resection for HCC
sectionToMerge.intro: Hepatic resection is a surgical option for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) in selected patients with adequate liver function. These FAQs explain what the surgery involves, who may be eligible, and what recovery typically looks like.

items.q: What is hepatic resection for HCC?
items.a: Hepatic resection is surgery to remove the part of the liver that contains a hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) tumour, along with a margin of healthy tissue. It aims to remove the cancer completely while leaving enough functioning liver behind. The liver can often regenerate after part is removed. Resection may be considered for selected patients with early-stage HCC and preserved liver function, based on tumour size, location, and specialist review.

items.q: How does liver resection surgery for HCC work?
items.a: Liver resection removes the tumour-bearing section of the liver, ranging from a small wedge to an entire lobe. Surgeons carefully divide liver tissue while controlling blood flow to reduce bleeding. The extent depends on tumour size, number, and position relative to major blood vessels. The operation may be done as open surgery or, in suitable cases, laparoscopically. The approach is decided by the surgical team after imaging and assessment of remaining liver volume.

items.q: What is the difference between minor and major liver resection?
items.a: Minor resection removes fewer than three liver segments, while major resection removes three or more, such as a full lobe. Major resections carry higher risks because less functioning liver remains afterward. The choice depends on tumour size, location near blood vessels, and how well the remaining liver is expected to work. Your surgical team estimates the future liver remnant before deciding, and this assessment should be discussed with a qualified hepatobiliary specialist.

items.q: Can hepatic resection cure hepatocellular carcinoma?
items.a: Hepatic resection offers a chance of long-term control for selected patients with early-stage HCC, but outcomes vary and cannot be guaranteed. When the tumour is fully removed with clear margins and liver function is preserved, some patients achieve extended survival. However, HCC can recur, especially in patients with underlying cirrhosis or hepatitis. Regular follow-up with imaging and blood tests is important, and prognosis should be discussed with the treating oncology team.

items.q: Who is eligible for hepatic resection for HCC?
items.a: Hepatic resection may be suitable for selected patients with early-stage HCC, a single tumour or limited disease, and well-preserved liver function. Eligibility depends on cancer stage, tumour location, the amount of healthy liver remaining, absence of major vessel invasion, and overall health. Patients with advanced cirrhosis or poor liver function may not be candidates. Final eligibility is decided by a hepatobiliary surgical team after imaging, blood tests, and specialist review.

items.q: What tests are needed before liver resection surgery?
items.a: Before liver resection, doctors usually order imaging such as CT or MRI scans, liver function blood tests, and tumour markers like alpha-fetoprotein (AFP). These assess tumour size, location, blood vessel involvement, and how much healthy liver would remain. Liver function scoring, such as the Child-Pugh classification, helps judge safety. Additional heart, lung, or fitness tests may be needed. The full workup is reviewed by the surgical and oncology team before planning.

items.q: How is liver function assessed before resection?
items.a: Liver function is assessed using blood tests, imaging, and scoring systems that estimate how well the liver works and how much healthy tissue will remain. The Child-Pugh score and measurements of the future liver remnant help predict whether the liver can cope after surgery. Signs of portal hypertension or advanced cirrhosis may reduce suitability. These assessments guide the surgical team and should always be interpreted by a qualified hepatobiliary specialist.

items.q: What are the risks and side effects of hepatic resection?
items.a: Hepatic resection carries risks including bleeding, infection, bile leakage, blood clots, and, in some cases, temporary or lasting liver dysfunction. Patients with cirrhosis face a higher chance of complications such as fluid buildup or liver failure. Risks depend on the extent of surgery, liver health, and overall fitness. Serious complications are uncommon in carefully selected patients, but all risks should be discussed in detail with the surgical team beforehand.

items.q: How long does liver resection surgery take?
items.a: Liver resection surgery usually takes between two and six hours, depending on tumour size, location, and how much liver is removed. Minor resections are generally quicker, while major resections near large blood vessels take longer. Laparoscopic (keyhole) approaches may add time but can shorten recovery in suitable cases. The exact duration varies for each patient, and the surgical team can give a clearer estimate after reviewing your imaging and treatment plan.

items.q: What does recovery after hepatic resection look like?
items.a: Recovery after hepatic resection typically involves a hospital stay of several days to about a week, followed by gradual recovery at home over several weeks. Early days focus on pain control, monitoring liver function, and slowly resuming eating and walking. Fatigue is common as the liver heals and regenerates. Most patients return to normal activity within four to eight weeks, though recovery varies with the extent of surgery and overall health.

items.q: How long is the hospital stay after liver resection?
items.a: The hospital stay after liver resection is usually around five to seven days, though it can be shorter for minor or laparoscopic resections and longer if complications occur. During this time, the team monitors liver function, pain, wound healing, and signs of bleeding or bile leakage. Patients are encouraged to walk early to reduce clot risk. The exact length depends on the surgery performed and individual recovery, as judged by the treating team.

items.q: Does the liver grow back after resection?
items.a: The liver has a natural ability to regenerate, and healthy liver tissue can grow to partly restore lost volume after resection. This regeneration usually begins within days and continues over several weeks to months. However, regeneration is less reliable in patients with cirrhosis or damaged liver, which is why liver function is carefully assessed beforehand. The degree of recovery varies for each patient and should be monitored by the treating medical team.

items.q: What follow-up is needed after HCC surgery?
items.a: After HCC surgery, regular follow-up is important because the cancer can return. Follow-up usually includes periodic imaging such as CT or MRI, blood tests including alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), and liver function monitoring, often every three to six months initially. This helps detect any recurrence early, when further treatment options may be possible. The exact schedule depends on your case and should be planned and adjusted by the treating oncology team.

items.q: How much does hepatic resection for HCC cost?
items.a: The cost of hepatic resection varies widely depending on the hospital, country, extent of surgery, tests, hospital stay, and any complications. Major resections and longer stays generally cost more than minor procedures. Costs may also include imaging, anaesthesia, intensive care, and follow-up. Because pricing depends on many factors, estimates should be confirmed directly with the treating hospital, and final costs cannot be guaranteed in advance without a full medical assessment.

items.q: Is hepatic resection available in India?
items.a: Hepatic resection for HCC is available at several specialised hepatobiliary and liver surgery centres in India, including hospitals with dedicated liver units. These centres may offer open and laparoscopic approaches for suitable patients. Availability and suitability depend on tumour stage, liver function, and specialist review of your reports. International patients often consider India for liver surgery, but acceptance and treatment planning are decided by the hospital and surgical team after reviewing medical records.

items.q: When is resection chosen over TACE or transplant for HCC?
items.a: Resection is often preferred for selected patients with a single tumour and preserved liver function, while transplant may be considered when cirrhosis is advanced or multiple tumours are present. TACE (transarterial chemoembolisation) may be used when surgery is not suitable or to control tumours before other treatment. The best option depends on tumour stage, liver health, and available donors, and should be decided by a multidisciplinary liver cancer team.

items.q: How can international patients access liver resection abroad?
items.a: International patients can access liver resection abroad by sharing medical reports with a hepatobiliary centre for review, obtaining a treatment estimate, and arranging travel and visas. Access depends on hospital acceptance, medical review, travel fitness, and the patient's condition, and cannot be guaranteed in advance. Planning should also cover an accompanying caregiver, length of stay, and follow-up care. A second opinion is often helpful before making decisions about surgery abroad.

items.q: What reports are needed to plan liver resection abroad?
items.a: To plan liver resection abroad, hospitals usually request recent imaging (CT or MRI scans), liver function and blood test results, tumour markers such as AFP, biopsy or pathology reports if available, and a summary of previous treatments. A clear medical history helps the surgical team assess suitability and estimate costs. Requirements vary between centres, and the treating team may ask for additional tests before confirming whether surgery is appropriate for your case.

items.q: How does CancerFax help patients with hepatic resection for HCC?
items.a: CancerFax helps patients organise medical reports, identify relevant specialists or liver surgery centres, estimate possible costs, and coordinate second opinions, appointments, travel, visa, and follow-up support. Treatment decisions are always made by the qualified oncology and surgical team after reviewing the patient's diagnosis, stage, biomarkers, previous treatment, liver function, and overall health. Support with logistics does not replace medical assessment, and eligibility for surgery is confirmed only after specialist review.
